title: p90-dollar-curve-ascii-walkthrough-may17-2027
content:
Goal:
Compare p90-driven cost/latency trade-offs across two common serving configs and produce an "ASCII-friendly" collateral piece that can be embedded in RFCs and Slack threads. Focus is on per-query dollar curve and operational sensitivity to KV cache hit rate and batch sizing.

Short summary (TL;DR):
- Setup A (opt-kernel + dynamic batching): consistently lower p90 across workloads, slightly higher per-token CPU/GPU utilization.
- Setup B (conservative kernels + small fixed batch): lower amortized cost for very large sessions but p90 suffers in bursty traffic.
- Key metric: p90 latency vs $/1M input+output tokens (operationalized as host+GPU amortized cost). See ASCII curves below.

Method & test harness:
- Workload: 52k synthetic conversational sessions sampled from production session-mix (mix: 45% short queries <64 tokens, 35% medium 64-512, 20% long >512).
- Models: open-13b-v2 (fp16, optimized kernels) and open-7b-quant (int8). Both warmed with 5K warmup requests.
- Hardware: A100-80GB (large pool), T4 (spot pool). Tests run with identical traffic replay for both configs.
- Batch policies: dynamic-batching (max 64, latency SLO 200ms) vs small-fixed-batch (max 8).
- KV cache hit-rate sweep: 10%, 40%, 70% (simulated by prefix reuse).
- Measurement window: 6-hour steady runs, sampling p50/p90/p99, and token consumption. Cost model: amortized GPU rental + infra overhead (internal cost model v2.1).

Representative numbers (A100 runs, avg over 3 repeats):
- Config A (opt-kernel + dynamic):
  p50: 32ms, p90: 68ms, p99: 185ms
  Cost: $22.5 per 1M tokens (input + output)
  Stability index (p99/p50): 5.8

- Config B (conservative + small-fixed):
  p50: 40ms, p90: 128ms, p99: 420ms
  Cost: $17.9 per 1M tokens
  Stability index: 10.5

Interpretation: Config A has ~26% higher nominal token cost but provides roughly 2x better p90 and ~2.3x tighter tail (stability index lower). For latency-sensitive endpoints the higher cost is frequently justified.

ASCII curve (p90 latency vs $/1M tokens) — each row is a config; columns are coarse cost buckets. X axis (cost buckets): [12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30] $/1M tokens. Numbers are median p90 in ms for that bucket (blank = not observed).

Legend: A = Config A (dynamic, opt-kernel), B = Config B (fixed, conservative)

            Cost ($/1M) ->  12   15   18   21   24   27   30
  Config A (A100)    |      95   82   74   68   66   63   61
  Config B (A100)    |  220  180  150  128  120  115  112
  Config A (T4)      |      140  118  100   92   89   86   83
  Config B (T4)      |  480  380  320  280  250  230  210

Notes on the table: buckets are generated by varying batch limits, kernel choice, and quantization. Config A dominates in p90 at modestly higher buckets. T4 behaves worse in tails, particularly for Config B.

Micro-insight: KV cache hit-rate sensitivity (example on A100):
  - At 10% hit-rate: p90(Config A) = 110ms, p90(Config B) = 240ms
  - At 40% hit-rate: p90(A) = 78ms, p90(B) = 135ms
  - At 70% hit-rate: p90(A) = 62ms, p90(B) = 102ms

This shows caching reduces both p90 and cost, but Config A extracts more marginal latency benefit (opt kernels exploit KV-prefetch better).

Operational implications (draft recommendations):
1) For public hosted endpoints with p90 SLOs <= 100ms: prefer Config A on A100 pools; accept ~20–30% higher cost if user-facing latency is critical.
2) For batch-heavy internal workloads or embeddings pipelines: Config B on T4 with aggressive packing may be more cost-effective if p90 SLOs are loose.
3) Hybrid routing policy: route 80% short-session traffic to A (dynamic) and long, background jobs to B. This preserves SLOs while reclaiming cost for long sessions.
4) Invest in adaptive kv-prefetch heuristics — results show large tail reductions with modest increases in cache hit ratio.

Visual snack (tiny sparkline of p90 over time for a burst window):
  time -> |00:00|00:05|00:10|00:15|00:20|00:25|00:30|
  A p90  ->  [———▁▂▃▅▇]   ~ stable after warmup (range 60–90ms)
  B p90  ->  [———▁▃▆▉▉]   wide spikes (range 120–520ms)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Edge cases for ultra-long context (>2K tokens) where memory remapping can flip cost curves. We did a limited sweep but need dedicated long-context runs.
- Interaction with HTTP chunking/streaming: our harness uses full response wait; streaming could alter p90 for perceived latency.
- Cost model sensitivity: using cloud spot pricing vs reserved changes the break-even point — need finance-backed Monte Carlo.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- 1-week long run with mixed spot/reserved node mix; produce cost CDF and re-evaluate bucket boundaries.
- Focused 2K-context run for long-session penalty and memory churn effects.
- Integrate a quick heuristic in runtime that flips kernel aggressiveness when session-length > 512 tokens and validate p90 impact.

Appendix: quick-run checklist for reproducibility:
- Replay id: replay-obs-20270517-3 (attach recording)
- Script: bench/replay/obs/p90-dollar-sweep.sh (PR linked above)
- Cost model file: cost-model/v2.1/assumptions.csv

Author notes: This doc is a compact collateral piece meant for product/solutions to communicate the practical p90 trade-off when choosing kernels and batching strategies. It should be reworked into a one-pager with a small SVG for external comms if stakeholders want a nicer visual.
